worksheet.title: Put It Back in Order
worksheet.subtitle: Fix the bug by re-ordering the blocks
worksheet.learning_goal: I can fix a program by putting the blocks back in order.

parts.title: Wrong order
parts.text: Sometimes the blocks are all right but in the WRONG ORDER. To fix it, put them back in the right order. Remember: a program must BEGIN with the start block.

parts.title: What is wrong?
parts.prompt: Look at Program 1. Why can't Bit run it? (Hint: where is the start block?)

parts.title: Put it in order
parts.prompt: Write the blocks in the right order so the program begins with the start block. Then run it — what number does Bit land on?

parts.title: You try — swap to fix
parts.prompt: Run Program 2 from 3. Forward 3 passes the end, so Bit stops on 5, then back 2 lands on 3 — not 4. Swap the two move blocks and run again. Where does Bit land now?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Code runs in order. If the blocks are in the wrong order, the program does the wrong thing — even when every block is right. Re-order them to fix the bug.

teacher_guide.title: Put It Back in Order
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 4. Put It Back in Order — Teacher Guide

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students fix bugs by re-ordering blocks: first by moving the start block to the top (a program must begin with start), then by swapping two move blocks whose order changes the result at the end of the path. Debugging by re-ordering a sequence is the heart of this subject and a clear C3.2 task, with a small C3.1 rewrite.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: cut Program 1's blocks apart so students can physically slide the start block to the top.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: point to Program 1. 'The start block is in the middle — Bit doesn't know where to begin. The start block must go first.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — the start block is not first. Exercise 2 — reorder to start at 1, forward 2, forward 1; Bit lands on 4.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — Program 2 lands on 3 because forward 3 hits the end first; swap to back 2, forward 3, and Bit lands on 4.
4. Connect: 'Same blocks, wrong order, wrong result — re-ordering is a kind of fix.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — the start block ('start at 1') is in the middle; a program must begin with the start block, so the order is wrong.
Ex 2 — right order: start at 1, forward 2, forward 1. Run: 1 → 3 → 4. Bit lands on 4.
Ex 3 — Program 2 buggy order (forward 3, back 2): 3 → 5 (stops at the end) → 3. Swapped (back 2, forward 3): 3 → 1 → 4. Bit lands on 4.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common idea in Ex 3: 'the blocks didn't change, so the answer can't change' — the end of the path is what makes the order matter; walk both orders to show it.
Simplify: do Program 1 only (move the start block to the top).
Extend: ask students to find another order of Program 2's blocks and check where Bit lands.
Success indicator: the child puts the start block first in Program 1 (lands on 4) and swaps the moves in Program 2 (lands on 4).
